⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The attacker wasn't able to access people's vaults.
  • According to recent reports, 1Password has admitted that an attacker was able to infiltrate its system and steal some customer data, but it has assured consumers in its announcement that their vaults and logins are safe.
  • According to recent reports, the attacker was then able to download customers' data, including people's names and email addresses, the dates their accounts were created and their last sign-in times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The attacker wasn't able to access people's vaults.

According to recent reports, 1Password has admitted that an attacker was able to infiltrate its system and steal some customer data, but it has assured consumers in its announcement that their vaults and logins are safe. On November 19, the manufacturer started investigating signs that an employee's corporate GitHub account had been compromised. The company found that the attacker used that account to access its source code and inject malicious code to its backend.

According to recent reports, the attacker was then able to download customers' data, including people's names and email addresses, the dates their accounts were created and their last sign-in times. They were also able to steal users' public keys, but 1Password said it has no impact to their security. While the bad actor was also able to steal source code from the firm itself, it doesn't contain customer data.

Sources indicate that "Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected," 1Password wrote. The service doesn't have access to customers' actual passwords, recovery keys and other credentials, as well as the secret keys that protect their vaults, so the attacker wasn't able to steal them. Since discovering the breach, 1Password has revoked the stolen token, disabled the affected GitHub account and added new detection tools for similar attacks.

Recent findings suggest that while 1Password stated that owners' vaults remain safe, the tech giant still advises being vigilant when it comes to phishing attempts. It warned that since users' emails were compromised in the breach, they could be used in attempts to grab people's passwords through fake account recovery and invitation emails.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".

Specifically, they remarked they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laÃ¯citÃ© - as a core component of its identity.

Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct.
  • According to recent reports, it’s an awkward stance for a organization whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules.
  • Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

According to recent reports, it’s an awkward stance for a organization whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

Recent findings suggest that “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly vital to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”.

Sources indicate that the consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”.

Sources indicate that plass states companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he stated, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”.

In a recent development, of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a manufacturer like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

According to recent reports, “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”.

Industry observers note that in that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the tech giant.

It has been revealed that if you’ve been curious about smart rings but have been put off by their high price tags, Black Friday is a good time to consider giving one a try. That’s because the Oura Ring 5, which we consider the best smart ring you can buy, has dropped to an all-time low of $299 ($100 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Oura’s online storefront for Black Friday.

According to recent reports, compared to the Ring 4, the Oura Ring 5 offers a thinner, lighter, and more durable design that’s more comfortable to wear throughout the day and while sleeping. Like its predecessor, it can track your sleep, activity, heart rate, and other health metrics, giving you insights into your overall well-being without requiring you to constantly check a screen. It also offers roughly the same battery life and sensors as the prior model, though its fresh charging case supports wireless charging. (Unfortunately, the case is right now sold separately for $99.).

Oura has also introduced several latest software features, including Health Radar, which looks for potentially significant changes in your health. You can also import medical lab results, track GLP-1 medications, and access AI-assisted medical guidance through Oura’s partnership with Counsel Health. My colleague Victoria Song appreciated how the latter makes it easier to connect with an actual doctor, though she found it better suited for quick medical questions than more serious health concerns.

However, none of these software features are exclusive to the Ring 5, and you’ll still need a $5.99 monthly Oura membership to access most of its health insights. Given how similar the two generations are, we wouldn’t recommend upgrading if you already own a Ring 4. But if you’re new to smart rings, the current discount makes Oura’s latest model much more attractive, especially since it’s only $50 more than the Ring 4’s starting price.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tame claims her "whole body was prickling with distress" over what Handbury remarked.

An Australian former media executive has admitted he stated a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.

Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.

In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame remarked she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.

Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.

Matt Handbury is the nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms.

Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.

She mentioned the encounter at the University of Newly introduced South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.

"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.

"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment.".

The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".

"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also stated: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'.

He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".

"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he noted, before signing off.

According to recent reports, handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.

Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".

It has been revealed that "It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?".

From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.

"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.

It has been revealed that "I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.

"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out.".

If you have been affected by any of the complications raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

Books, bikes, and The Burbs: These are Ars staff’s holiday gift picks for 2026

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the holiday shopping season is upon us, and as is our custom, we’re here with a list of Ars staffers’ favorite recent purchases that could make good gifts. (Or maybe they might be a gift you get yourself!).

Recent findings suggest that rather than try to write a definitive “best gifts for your sister or brother” type of guide, we simply polled Ars staffers on stuff they’ve actually bought this year that they recommend. The thinking is that if we’re into it, hopefully some of you or your friends or family might be. As such, there’s no rhyme or reason to these selections, really; it’s just a list of stuff we bought that we’re happy about. It’s heavy on interesting books and cycling accessories, but there are some gadgets and the like in here, too.

For each gadget (or whatever else it might be), we have a brief description of how or why we’ve been using this particular thing and why we would recommend it. Our picks are ordered by price, from lowest to highest. Note, though, that the prices of these products are listed as they were when the list was written. Online retailers often adjust prices frequently, especially around Black Friday, so just a heads up: The price might be different by the time you read this.

Also, a callout to the Ars commentariat: If you have your own holiday buying recommendations, feel free to share them. We or some fellow readers might take your advice if you suggest something good! Happy holidays!

Dungeon Crawler Carl by Matt Dinniman – $13.

I understand the convenience and space-savings that e-readers bring. My 2011 Kindle Touch goes with me everywhere I carry my travel backpack, but I’m still a softy for physical books when I’m sitting at home on a lazy Sunday. What started as something of a fanfic send-up of LitRPGs has quickly blossomed into a massive sensation of a series filled with far more depth, heart, and character than the initial premise might indicate. Author Matt Dinniman has an accessible style that will grip any reader with a taste for whimsical adventure. Just be warned that if you leave the books under the tree, you might not see much of the recipient until New Year’s.

Undersea War: The Battle to Control the Cables and Pipelines That Connect Our World by Elisabeth Braw– $30.

Lightning Beneath the Sea: The Race to Wire the World and the Dawn of the Information Age by James M. Tabor– $32.

It has been revealed that two excellent books that help describe how the Internet’s undersea backbone became a globe-spanning reality were published in 2026. Together, they form a great gift pairing for anyone interested in how humanity first achieved near-instantaneous communication across the world’s oceans—and how the first trans-Atlantic telegraph cable paved the way for a global network of subsea data cables that now faces growing risks from geopolitical conflicts.

James Tabor’s Lightning Beneath the Sea dives into the astounding real-life story of how American entrepreneur Cyrus Field, lacking in expertise but driven by personal fervor, set out to achieve peace on Earth by laying a 2,000-mile telegraph cable made of copper across the Atlantic seafloor in 1866.

To pull off the feat, Field managed to convince some of the greatest innovators and scientific luminaries of his day, such as Samuel F.B. Morse, Lord Kelvin, and Michael Faraday, to join his venture. He also refitted the SS Great Eastern steamship, the largest passenger liner ship built to date, as a cable-laying vessel.

In a recent development, that first ocean-spanning telegraph cable gave rise to more such cables for transmitting messages around the world. Eventually copper gave way to a network of subsea fiber-optic cables that became the Internet’s undersea backbone, and the modern world also became interlinked with submarine power cables and underwater pipelines for carrying oil and gas.

But all that undersea infrastructure is now facing growing danger from the threat of deliberate sabotage, as described in Elisabeth Braw’s book Undersea War. Her book provides a sobering but enlightening look at why subsea cables and pipelines are becoming more tempting targets amid rising geopolitical tensions and conflicts—and how governments and companies are responding to recent cable-cutting incidents around the world.

Read Ars Technica’s Q&A with Elisabeth Braw about Undersea War.

The Burbs Collector’s Edition 4K Blu-ray – $32.

According to recent reports, it’s a little-remembered film for most people, but I absolutely love The Burbs. Sure, it’s more Halloween fare than Christmas, but last year I picked The Thing, so clearly “1980s movies for October” is my December viewing MO.

Sources indicate that starring Tom Hanks, Carrie Fisher, and Corey Feldman, this is a dry, hilarious send-up of suburban life with a horror-adjacent mystery that keeps you guessing. (It’s not scary, though.) I hardly ever hear anyone else talk about this movie, but I love it, and it only recently came out in 4K, so I’m taking this opportunity to shout it out.

How Apollo Flew to the Moon by David Woods – $35.

If you’re a technically minded Ars reader looking for a nice book to snuggle down with over the holidays, David Woods’ How Apollo Flew to the Moon could be just the thing. (There’s also an audiobook version.) Woods has an accessible style that breaks down complex engineering challenges and their solutions into easily digestible chunks that clarify without oversimplifying. He uses that style to take readers on a detailed trip through the machinery of Project Apollo, from the launch facilities and Mission Control all the way to the specific mechanics of how to navigate to and land on the Moon—and, from there, how to return safely to Earth.

It has been revealed that ever wondered about the insane engineering that let the Saturn V’s first stage burn almost 15 tons of fuel every second as it powered the crew into orbit? Or how to pinpoint a spacecraft’s centimeter-precise distance from Earth on its way to the Moon? Or how Apollo crews tracked their own position with stellar navigation, using sextants and star sightings? Or what a REFSMMAT is, or how television transmissions from the Moon worked, or how they got those crazy lunar buggies onto the Moon’s surface? All these questions and more are given beautifully complete and technically satisfying answers, suitable for both the curious layperson and also the interested engineer. Grab this book and stun your family at Christmas with amazing Apollo trivia—as a bonus, you’ll have the knowledge to make your “We never landed on the Moon!” conspiracy theorist uncle so angry that he stops talking and watches football in grumpy silence! Everyone wins!

It has been revealed that as someone who grew up in the classic era of 16-bit SNES RPGs, this 40th anniversary tribute to the series’ history is everything I could have ever wanted in a modern entry. I haven’t properly played through a Final Fantasy entry since the days of Final Fantasy X on PlayStation 2, but when friends kept nudging me that this was the perfect “Nick game,” I figured I should probably take a look. There’s a free six-hour demo available on supported platforms if you’re still on the fence about picking this one up, but don’t be surprised if you end up grabbing a copy for yourself.

Govee Star Light Projector (Nebula Effect) – $70.

For the past couple of years, I’ve been transforming my tiny office into a sanctuary in the evenings, since I do most of my writing (and gaming) in here then. It started with Govee Hexa panels, then came an RGB TV backlight, then colorful smart bulbs for the built-in light fixtures. I topped it off with the Star Light projector, which coats the ceiling in a soothing, ever-shifting, immersive stars-and-nebula effect.

It’s probably not for everybody, but my office is tiny, and I spend a lot of time here both for work and for fun. Tapping a button to completely shift the vibe is surprisingly effective at making it a room I don’t mind spending time in even after I’ve been working in it all day.

Easily my favorite impulse purchase of 2026, the FM-1 is a great gift for curious tinkerers and experienced musicians alike. At around $70 or less, you don’t have to break the bank to get fiddling. A perfectly decent stock synthesizer on its own, the real fun starts when you begin experimenting with the community firmware packages that transform the synth into anything from a multi-track groovebox to one of the more hilarious ways that I’ve ever tried to play Doom.

Trek BellBeats digital bike bell and speaker – $125One of the great things about cycling is the chance to be alone with my thoughts—just me and my bike. But that can be too much of a good thing on longer zone 2 rides and centuries. Sporting the size and shape of an old-school bicycle bell, the Trek BellBeats is a safer alternative to donning headphones while on the bike.BellBeats pair with your phone via Bluetooth and will play music at a volume loud enough to enjoy your tunes or hear navigation prompts, but they are not so loud that the music drowns out traffic (or the radar on your bike computer). They can be mounted on just about any non-aero handlebars, charge over USB-C, and offer up to six hours of playtime. And as a bonus, they double as a bicycle bell.

I use Bluetooth headphones most of the time, but frustratingly, they don’t work with voice chat on the PlayStation 5, and I needed a good-quality headset for my Friday night multiplayer gaming sessions.

I’ve always liked Fractal Design’s PC cases, so I decided to roll the dice on their affordable-for-the-quality, over-ear headphones. They support Bluetooth, but they also have a USB dongle, so they can be used for voice chat on game consoles, too.

I was surprised by how much I like them, and despite buying them just for the PS5, I’ve ended up using them in other contexts. Part of that is because they’re very comfortable, and the design avoids my glasses frames well.

I also like that, although they are gaming headphones with all the expected bells and whistles for that, they don’t have an over-the-top design.

If you’re in the market for mid-range wireless gaming headphones that look like something you could actually wear in public without embarrassment, these fit the bill so far.

Povec C1 Performance Sunglasses – $250Photochromic sunglasses are incredibly useful for outdoor workouts. Two of the most popular bike trails near me run through forest preserves, and the lighting changes steadily as the forest canopy closes in or spreads out. My default sunglasses are a cheap, $28 pair from Rockbros.Unlike other photochromic glasses, which change tints via a pokey chemical reaction, the Povec C1 uses a battery to switch between tints in a second. All the rider (or runner) needs to do is swipe the right temple and the lenses will darken or lighten almost instantaneously. The C1 charges via a small USB-C port, and the Povec claims 28 days of battery life with four hours of daily usage. I’ve used them off and on for about six weeks and have only had to charge them once.

The C1 comes in three frame colors and either Green Revo or Gold Revo glasses and is an excellent stocking stuffer for the runner, cyclist, or skier in your life.

Recent findings suggest that garmin Varia RCT715 radar camera tail light – $300Last spring, a friend of mine was the victim of a hit-and-run while on a ride. Although she wasn’t seriously hurt, her brand-upcoming bike was totaled. The driver got an unwelcome surprise a couple of days later when the police knocked on his front door and arrested him. My friend was riding with a Garmin Varia RCT715, a combination taillight and radar with a camera. The 1080p/30 fps camera captured the car’s license plate, making it possible for the police to identify the driver.More than 90 percent of my riding is on roads, and I don’t feel fully comfortable without my Varia. I have it paired with my Garmin Edge 1050 bike computer, but it will work with most other brands via ANT+. The Varia detects approaching vehicles at 140 meters, and I have it set to record video starting when a car is detected and for 30 seconds after it passes. Battery life is up to six hours, depending on whether the taillight is solid or flashing, and video is saved on a 16GB microSD memory card.

Hiplock DX1000 Bike Lock – $380.

My YouTube algorithm has recently fed me videos of testers using an angle grinder to cut through decent bike locks in under a minute. I’ve never seen an angle grinder-assisted theft in person, but I’ve seen enough heaps of bike parts around town to know people’s rides are getting jacked somewhere. As someone known to be neurotic about leaving my bike outside my purview, I’m looking for added security measures to ease my stress.Enter the Hiplok, which, according to the tests I’ve watched, will turn multiple angle-grinder blades to dust. Do bike thieves carry several discs, and will they spend about 15 minutes trying to break this lock? I don’t know, but I have my doubts. At nearly $400, it’s about as expensive as it gets to secure your ride, but when your bike tops $5,000, it’s probably worth the added theft deterrence and peace of mind.

According to recent reports, santa left this one last year, and the rest of my handheld collection has felt neglected since. Sporting a Snapdragon 8 Elite (now dubbed the Dragonwing Q8) chip, excellent ergonomics, and a 6-inch 120Hz AMOLED screen, it’s the perfect balance between size and horsepower. The Android unit is capable enough to play most anything you can throw at it, without the bulk of a Steam Deck or the bloat of a Windows handheld. Thanks to things like Proton, FEX translation, and software like DroidDeck or GameNative, there isn’t much I can’t use it for. Streaming consoles or PC gaming? Check. Access to Steam, GOG, Epic, Rockstar libraries? Check. High-end native Android gaming? Yup. Emulate anything under the sun? You’re covered there, too. The latest Odin 3 Portal hardware revision gets a larger 7-inch screen and a base RAM configuration of 12GB over the original model’s 8GB. I may have to ask Mr. Claus about an upgrade….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The website does not store payment, government ID or financial information, so none of that was exposed.

Video game-logging site Backloggd has urged customers to change their passwords after announcing a security breach. The website's administrator MrProg wrote in a post dated November 25 that "someone exploited a bug in Backloggd to gain access to the site's admin tools." As a result, the infiltrator was able to access usernames, email addresses, hashed passwords and the IP addresses users signed in from. Payment information was not affected as that's handled through Patreon.

According to recent reports, backloggd admin MrProg mentioned that, while the platform uses "a strong hashing method" to mask login credentials, "weak or common passwords can sometimes be guessed from their hashes." As such, it's best for Backlogged customers to change their password for the site and anywhere else they use the same one. (Take this as a reminder to opt for a strong, unique password on every single service you use. A password manager can help handle that, while passkeys and multi-factor authentication add extra layers of security to your accounts.).

MrProg apologized for the security incident. The admin took Backloggd offline as soon as they became aware of the situation to fix the bug and lock out the attacker, who also hid games and restricted some accounts. All users will need to log back in, and MrProg noted they're reverting all the changes the attacker made.

According to recent reports, "Your game logs, reviews and lists all remain intact," MrProg added. "I'm at the moment seeking legal guidance to ensure I handle this with absolute care and will share a full notice with more details soon." The site's operator has "already added stricter access to the admin tools and will continue to commit to stronger security features to help protect your account.".

Backloggd is a site on which people can log and rate games they play, in a similar fashion to what Letterboxd does for movies. Users can track their game collection, review what they've played, create lists and follow their friends' gaming progress. Backloggd has been around for eight years and it hit 1 million users this month. A native mobile app is coming next year. Those who back the site via Patreon can now check out a beta version of the Android app.

Thailand is pushing its neighbor Myanmar to take on unregulated mining.

According to recent reports, A toxic border river is putting lives and livelihoods at risk in northern Thailand. The Kok River, once rich in fish, is now polluted with arsenic, mercury, and other hazardous contaminants.

It has been revealed that the reason is the mining activity in the militia-controlled regions of Myanmar. Most of these mines are located in Shan state, where civil war has raged since the 2021 military coup.

The mining activity is driven in part by China's dominant rare earth industry.

Bangkok this week hosted the first Thai-Myanmar working group where it said tests proved rare-earth and gold mines in Myanmar were the reason of the pollution downstream. China was also present in the talks.

The two sides agreed to joint water sampling on the Kok and Sai rivers. This will cover 12 water sampling locations and is expected to begin between December and January.

But no public agreement was made about Thailand's request for a six-month suspension of mining operations.

The talks follow the suspension of tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district earlier this month, near the Myanmar border, after arsenic levels were found to be nearly 30 times higher than government limits.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Bangkok is also seeking China's help in pressuring private Chinese operators, given its position as the main importer of rare-earth materials from Myanmar, as the issue grows increasingly urgent after months of concern.

Authorities this week urged residents to avoid eating certain shellfish and other river species after tests detected dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in northern and northeastern Thailand.

"Arsenic does not come from nature, it came from mining sites. The source was from (Myanmar's) Shan state, no-one disagrees," Thai Deputy ​Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said at the joint talks.

However, finding a solution remains a challenge.

Thanapon Piman, senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), told AFP, "This is going to be a first step to agree on the evidence, otherwise you cannot move to the next step, like stopping mining activity.”.

But Myanmar intervening to stop mining would be "really difficult," he added.

Several ethnic armed groups have been active in the region for decades, while the civil war is still ongoing.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Thai authorities point to two gold mines across the border from Mae Sai as the main contributors to elevated arsenic levels in the Sai River.

The broader region is divided among various groups, including Myanmar's military and the United Wa State Army, an ethnic armed group closely aligned with China.

The main mining belts are presently outside the control of Myanmar's military-backed government, including sites in Shan State.

Thai authorities are also seeking to assess whether pollutant mines are under the control of Myanmar's government or other entities, Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan told Reuters.

"We also would like them to check whether they can control every mine or they cannot. If they cannot, we will ask China to help,” he said.

A spokesperson from China's foreign ministry told AFP that Beijing "pays close attention" to the pollution issue and would provide technical support.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿.

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

When Keychron unveiled its $90 G6 HE gaming mouse, I immediately thought, “Cool! A cheaper alternative to the pricey $180 Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike.” Logitech’s innovation with the Superstrike is using magnetic Hall effect switches for a user-adjustable mouse click depth, with haptic vibrations mimicking the tactile click feel. The Keychron G6 HE, as its name indicates, also uses Hall effect switches for that same kind of customization. But something felt immediately off as I began testing it.

The mouse’s shape and design are very reminiscent of Logitech G Pro models, with more colorful flair. The magnetic switches are there and easily customizable (through a browser-based app, no less). But the clicks? The clicks are all wrong.

It has been revealed that the left and right mouse buttons on the G6 HE use Keychron’s MagOptic switches, which are both magnetic Hall effect and optical. They click just like any standard mouse, regardless of where you set the actuation point. There are no fancy haptics on the Keychron. If you set the buttons to a shallow hair-trigger depth, you’ll register a press before you actually feel or hear any click. Set the depth for a very heavy press, and the mouse clicks before it actually registers. That… kind of defeats the purpose here.

It has been revealed that there’s not much point in tuning the actuation depth of the G6 HE’s buttons if the click feel doesn’t match it. I suppose it’s still nice to have a hair-trigger-like setting for taking faster single shots in an FPS, but not feeling anything when you shoot is weird. And it gets frustrating when using the G6 HE as a regular mouse for productivity — like you’re getting phantom clicks as you mouse around your computer. At least I can feel my accidental clicks when using a Logitech Superstrike with the action set too high, and I know I’m to blame for leaving the mouse on my try-hard settings.

I reached out to Keychron for the reasoning behind the G6 HE’s magnetic-but-not-haptic setup, and cofounder Fab Chan stated, “There are two reasons for this design. First, many owners still prefer the feel of a traditional click over haptics. Second, a haptic motor adds weight, and for this model we prioritized a lighter design. That said, we’re planning a model with haptic feedback. It will be slightly heavier than the G6 HE, and we’ll share more details soon.”.

The G6 HE is a lightweight mouse. It’s only 49g with its battery, or 40g in wired mode with the battery removed. The Logitech X2 Superstrike is 60g, and the newer X3 Superstrike is 59g — each still pretty light. If you ignore all the Hall effect stuff and just use the G6 HE as a regular mouse, it has some things going for it over the Superstrikes. In addition to its lighter build and much lower price, it feels a tiny bit comfier in my hand, thanks to its side walls that curve slightly inward at the bottom.

In a recent development, one of its best features is hot-swappable batteries. From my time testing Angry Miao’s AM Infinity Mouse, I know that once you can pop out a magnetic battery pack and quickly swap it, you never want to go back to plugging in your mouse to charge. You can also get the G6 HE in black with a standard built-in rechargeable battery for $15 less, but I don’t think that’s enough savings to forgo the convenience of hot-swap batteries.

According to recent reports, the G6 HE’s charging base doubles as the wireless receiver, and of course it’s lit up with customizable RGB lighting. It has four programmable buttons for on-the-fly changes to things like DPI, lighting, mouse profiles, or just about anything else you want to program. The browser-based Keychron Launcher software is robust and makes tinkering with the G6 HE or its base very easy. And for some reason, the receiver / charging base is designed like a vacuum tube, which is fun, but it means you’re unscrewing its clear housing to access the battery — a little tedious.

It has been revealed that I can’t shake my disappointment with the G6 HE’s lackadaisical magnetic switch implementation. Keychron seems proud of the fancy MagOptic Switch it put into the G6 HE, even going so far as to call it “next gen,” but this mouse seems a jack of all trades and master of none. The G6 HE is cheaper than most other mice with hot-swap batteries — which can still make it worthwhile if you don’t care about all the Hall effect stuff — but that is its lone saving grace.

According to recent reports, we’ll have to wait and see if Keychron’s follow-up model with haptics can properly compete with the Superstrike mice and their hallmark feature. I’m excited to see where Hall effect tech goes in mice, and how more companies can evolve it, but the G6 HE is a half-measure.

Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge.

Google will soon share Android developers' addresses publicly

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Their phone numbers and addresses will be published globally, starting on March 1, 2027.
  • Starting on March 1, 2027, Google will display Android developers' phone numbers and addresses with their apps, and users everywhere will be able to see them.
  • Sources indicate that google, like Apple, now requires developers to declare whether they're a trader under UK laws and the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA).

Their phone numbers and addresses will be published globally, starting on March 1, 2027.

Starting on March 1, 2027, Google will display Android developers' phone numbers and addresses with their apps, and users everywhere will be able to see them. As The Elec has reported, this decision has been met with criticism, specifically from smaller developers who operate out of their homes. Some of them have been opting to rent offices just so they won't have to declare their real address. "Disclosing developers' home addresses amounts to an invasion of privacy," one independent developer told the publication.

Sources indicate that google, like Apple, now requires developers to declare whether they're a trader under UK laws and the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA). The organization says they have to classify themselves as a trader if they intend to earn money from their apps in any way on a regular basis, and if they already have a consistent frequency of transactions. Developers will have to make their declaration by February 1, 2027. Once they classify themselves as a trader, they'll have to submit their business identity, phone number and address, which Google will display to customers everywhere. Users in the UK and the European Economic Area will also see their business details and self-certification.

If they fail to comply with these requirements, Google could block their updates from rolling out. Ultimately, the company could remove their apps from the Play store, not just in Europe, but in all regions around the world. The Verge notes that Google doesn't accept PO Boxes for an address like Apple does, forcing people to think of ways to protect their identifying information while still earning money from their apps. Apple also won't be displaying developers' phone numbers and addresses globally like Google intends to do, only in the European countries covered by the laws requiring them.

#219131. Breaking: Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1902 w)

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company.
  • Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a firm call contained in a federal lawsuit.
  • Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a firm call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”.

Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”.

Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”.

According to recent reports, president Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

Industry observers note that fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

In a recent development, it’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”.

Documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

According to recent reports, “It’s just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The tech giant starts making decisions not based on what’s best for the company in the short or long term, what’s best for shareholders, but what’s best for politics and what the government is demanding.”.

“That’s not what you want from any firm,” he adds. “When you’re talking about the world’s most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that’s a huge problem.”.

Recent findings suggest that representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

The parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the company’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office.

During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research.

It has been revealed that at the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, says the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times.) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “a horrible, horrible thing.” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration remarked it was renegotiating the deals.

The same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s newly introduced CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing’s military. Tan’s former firm, Cadence Design Systems, pleaded guilty to violating US sanctions by selling semiconductor designs to a restricted Chinese military university, and agreed to pay more than $140 million in fines. Tan was never personally charged, but the violations happened while he was the CEO.

According to recent reports, two weeks later, the president was watching Maria Bartiromo’s show on the Fox Business Network. It mentioned a letter a senator had sent Intel about the China ties. Trump posted, “The CEO of INTEL is highly CONFLICTED and must resign, immediately. There is no other solution to this problem.”.

Tan went to the Oval Office on August 11 to see if there was, in fact, another solution. He got 40 minutes with the president, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Recent findings suggest that tan claimed his experience in China was a strength, not a detriment. According to the book Regime Change, Tan argued that there was no way he could’ve known about every one of the deals his many companies made; Trump, who had his own sprawling business empire, surely knew what that was like. Tan promised to give up his holdings in China, according to a letter Tan shared with Intel’s board, and put any proceeds into a blind trust.

Recent findings suggest that “The primary goal was to eliminate any worries about Lip-Bu himself, his Cadence background, and his investments with China,” according to a source with knowledge of the matter. But there were major financial concerns for Intel, too. “We had declining revenues and needed money.”.

In a recent development, neither Tan’s letter, excerpted in the complaint, nor Trump’s social media posts praising the CEO after the meeting mentioned anything about giving the government a chunk of the manufacturer. Yet Trump later insisted that a deal had been cooked up right then and there. “He came in, he saw me, we talked for a while. I liked him a lot, I thought he was very good,” the president told The Wall Street Journal. “I mentioned, ‘You know what? I think the United States should be given 10% of Intel.’ And he said, ‘I would consider that.’”.

“I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy,” Trump later recalled.

Recent findings suggest that according to the court filing’s review of Intel’s internal documents, Shapiro—a former partner at the New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—made a verbal offer on August 18. Ultimately, in exchange for the cut of Intel, the Trump administration would free up the $8.9 billion US government grants that it had already won. They wanted about a tenth of the tech giant’s stock for free, in exchange for Washington keeping the commitment it had already made.

Sources indicate that then came the call in which Shapiro insisted there was no room for negotiation. “The board needs to consider,” he said, according to Intel’s summary of his remarks included in the court documents, the “benefits of having a friend in this administration and what the administration can do to help Intel (including with customers).”.

In a recent development, intel’s board met, and decided they hated the deal. “The economic terms that had been proposed [by] the Administration were not, in their current form, attractive to the organization,” minutes of the meeting, reprinted in the lawsuit, noted.

But they went ahead with it anyway. Paisner’s lawyers say in the court documents the board took the offer thrust forward by the administration. Intel’s attorneys disagree, arguing in their motion to dismiss that there was some back-and-forth deal-making, and it made the agreement more favorable to the company. The grants became “immediately available” while “strategically aligning the interests of Intel’s stockholders and the US Government.”.

On August 25, Lutnick released a video with Tan, sitting side-by-side on cushioned chairs. “I really look forward to have the US government be my shareholder,” Tan turned to Lutnick and mentioned. “And we can work together and make Intel great again.”.

Inside the tech giant, the video was “a surprise to everyone,” according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. Some employees joked that it was reminiscent of a “hostage video.”.

Not long after that, Nvidia—led by Tan’s friend Jensen Huang—made a $5 billion investment in Intel. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted. “Who would not want to make deals like that?”.

Deals, plural. On the day Tan was hauled to the Oval Office, Trump announced that his administration had been negotiating separately with Huang. The Nvidia leader was beyond eager to sell more of his semiconductors to China. “And I said, if I’m going to do that, I want you to pay us as a country something,’” Trump said. They settled on 15 percent of all sales of the H20 model chip. Months after that, they cut a second deal: a 25 percent bounty on sales of Nvidia’s even-more advanced H200 chips.

In their lawsuit against Nvidia, Paisner’s attorneys argue the surcharges amount to “unlawful taxes,” and that the board’s “decisions to enter into such agreements are the product of mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duty.”.

In court, NVIDIA’s lawyers insisted that the firm “did not enter into any illegal ‘agreement’ with the government but instead engaged with the government and stated that it would comply with federal regulations.” Moreover, the attorneys say Paisner is trying to make a political point, rather than a legal one. “When asked about his purpose in bringing this action,” they write, “Paisner was candid: ‘It’s to make a public point of how NVIDIA conducts itself.’”.

The attorneys wrote this in May, months before Nvidia’s and Huang’s recent drama. Last week, board chair Harvey Jones noted on the company’s quarterly earnings call that it did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” citing his “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” (Not to mention mounting evidence that the company’s most sophisticated chips were making their way to China, in violation of US law.) But, according to The Fresh York Times, after days of pressure from top administration officials, the company and the government essentially struck a deal Sunday night to reinstate Huang.

“Don’t think for a second that politics ever play a role in this company, not even a little bit,” Huang noted during his first company-wide meeting after rejoining the company, WIRED reported. “We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”.

Additional reporting by Lauren Goode.

Tech Report: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.
  • Recent findings suggest that the FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences.
  • The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

Recent findings suggest that the FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real blueprint.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also stated the proposal “risks real harm.”.

The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr noted in a statement that the action “opens a bold latest frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

It has been revealed that musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”.

This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

Sources indicate that the company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

Industry observers note that spaceX has said it prepares to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much.﻿.

You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much.﻿.

Aside from dealing with my calendar, there’s one thing I want AI to do: tell me if I’m about to miss the bus.

What I need is a widget. It needs to tell me real-time arrivals for the bus stop near my house. Tapping around on my phone screen to open the right app and select my stop will slow me down enough to miss a bus. I need glanceable information, and I hoped that Android’s vibe-coded widget feature could help me out here. It hasn’t, to my disappointment, but I still had a good time cooking up other widgets.

Sources indicate that google revealed the ability to create custom widgets using AI back at I/O in the spring. It’s called Create My Widget, and it’s part of Android’s suite of “Gemini Intelligence” features. It’s in beta, and only just started rolling out to Pixel phones earlier this month. I was hyped. Not only does this feature raise tantalizing questions like “What is an app?” and “Where does the app live?” — stuff we live for here at The Verge dot com — it has potential to help me make my home screen ridiculous.

I fired it up on a Pixel 11 Pro and cooked up my first few widgets, including one that reveals a different quote from Jurassic Park every hour — the original film, not any of the sequels, naturally. It took about 20 seconds to make, and it rules. Tapping the widget opens a thread in r/MovieQuotes, so there’s not much software magic going on under the hood, evidently. But did it bring me real joy to read the words “That is one big pile of shit,” on my home screen? It did.

I also made a widget that will display the words “Tut tut, looks like rain” whenever it’s raining. This is silly, and it accomplishes nothing except making me happy. I couldn’t think of anything clever it should say when there’s no rain, so it just indicates “No rain right now” otherwise. But I live in Seattle, so I’ll get a lot of mileage out of this widget.

The create-a-widget interface suggests a few ideas and categories, leaning on more practical uses like habit trackers and recipe inspiration. Fine, I’ll try something normal, I thought. I’m trying to get better about my daily mental health walk, so I had it make a widget for logging a week’s worth of walks. I was hoping for something visual that would trick my little monkey brain into keeping a streak going. Instead, I got something simply labeled “Log Walk” that triggers Gemini to add a walk to my calendar when I tap it. At least Gemini suggested the extra step of creating a checklist where I could mark off the days of the week as I completed my little walk.

According to recent reports, it took me a minute to get my head around it, but many of the widgets are basically little prompt shortcuts for Gemini. You tap one, it pulls up the Gemini interface on your home screen, thinks for a while, then comes up with whatever you were asking for. The kinds of widgets you can make also seem to fit into some well-defined templates. You can create a widget that displays a countdown to a holiday or certain event on your calendar. You can show a recent score and upcoming game time for your favorite sports team. For anything more open ended, your widget will pull from Google search results (suggest a different three-ingredient cocktail recipe every day, for example) or prompt Gemini to figure it out for you. I was hoping for mini apps I could customize to my liking, but this is more of a one-size-fits-all feature. Fair, I guess.

I was hoping for mini apps I could customize to my liking, but this is more of a one-size-fits-all feature.

Sources indicate that that’s why my bus schedule widget didn’t really work out. I asked for a list of real-time arrivals; it gave me a tile that reads “Bus Arrivals” and uses Gemini to search for arrival times for the stop I specified. Gemini is helpful for some things but useless for this; it gives me a wordy response about how often the bus runs and when I might expect it to arrive based on the schedule. Not what I had in mind. On the bright side, my Jurassic Park quote widget had some words of wisdom for me: “Life, uh, finds a way.” That’ll do for now.

How New York reacted to postponement of Macy's parade.

Touring musicians from across the US who descended on Fresh York City to perform at the Macy's Thanksgiving parade have turned to fundraising to cover their costs, after getting stuck when the event was rearranged due to a storm.

Sources indicate that A band from Texas told the BBC's US partner, CBS News, it had raised some $350,000 (Â£267,000) to pay for an extended stay for its 500 members. It saluted the kindness of its supporters.

A group of student musicians from Hawaii, meanwhile, voiced their relief after friends and family rallied around to cover their additional hotel, coach and meal costs.

The parade, a famous annual event, is now scheduled to take place on Saturday.

Earlier this week, organisers said they would it push it back by two days, in part due to the concerns around flying giant inflatables in strong winds.

The balloons were temporarily deflated for a few days - and so too were the spirits of those who had journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed, although it was suspended altogether during World War Two.

Industry observers note that each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, some of them from high schools, to provide music for the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions of people in person and on TV.

Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather.

The leader of the Texas band described his emotions as costs for his delegation were met.

"It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band at Pearland High School, near Houston, in Texas, told CBS.

Demkovich mentioned contributions had arrived from businesses and individuals in the band's home community, with the help of a social media push.

The Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Texas - pictured rehearsing earlier this week - said it raised hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Meanwhile, the Hawaii group, the the NÄ Koa AliÊ»i HawaiÊ»i All-State Marching Band, mentioned it would still be able to participate in the parade, as a result of the efforts of families, friends, and other supporters who raised more than $500,000.

Speaking to the BBC earlier on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.

The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It had travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.

"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional, for our students," Badua stated.

But the musicians sprang into action rapidly, he mentioned. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".

The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he remarked.

New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macyâs Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Badua was hopeful his group would get the same experience he had when he first performed in the parade in 2003, as student drum major.

"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great.".

Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it was trying to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.

"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Prof Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.

While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain that were brought by a storm to eastern areas of the US.

Hundreds of thousands of homes lost power, and coastal areas were flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.
  • Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P noted in a statement.
  • The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P noted in a statement.

The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia unveiled plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.

A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

The latest super-rugged wearable from Apple features better battery life than the previous version, plus AI-powered features like Siri Recap also available on the Series 12.

According to recent reports, the Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review.

According to recent reports, an HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to reveals like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly, ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.

Compared to the last-gen base Kindle model (currently $119.99), the Paperwhite is a much better value. It features waterproofing, better battery life, faster page-turning speeds, and a higher pixel density screen that’s slightly larger (7 inches vs. 6 inches).

It has been revealed that do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.

In a recent development, sony’s XM4 noise-canceling headphones were so good, the tech giant brought them back with a few minor improvements. They still offer great ANC, a timeless foldable design, and delivering performance nearly on par with Sony’s newer flagships at a fraction of the cost.

The water-resistant Sonos Play sits between the Roam 2 and Move 2, offering a balance of portability and room-filling sound. It delivers up to 24 hours of battery life, with a built-in loop for easy carrying. You can also use it as a power bank and pair it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when Wi-Fi isn’t available. Read our review.

In a recent development, apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

Sources indicate that amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.

It has been revealed that rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.

The P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. That includes certain cameras, tablets, and drones with a microSD USH-I slot.

Apple’s 11th-gen iPad is the successor to the previous 10-gen model. It has a newly introduced A16 chip and few other changes — and is the only Apple tablet to not support Apple Intelligence.

Industry observers note that peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. In a recent development, the Ring 5 is a fantastic entry point for new owners. While short on improvements over its thicker predecessor, it’s hard not to appreciate that it manages to deliver similar battery life despite being thinner. Read our review.

It has been revealed that 007 First Light, a third-person stealth action game from the studio behind Hitman, is arguably the best action game we’ve played this year. According to recent reports, birdfy’s metal smart bird feeder features a wide-angle 4K camera that lets you get an up-close look at visiting birds, along with a 1.8-liter seed capacity and a built-in solar panel for charging. Sources indicate that roku now makes some of the most affordable, yet feature-packed 4K OLED TVs available for gamers or movie lovers looking for a major TV upgrade under $1,000. In a recent development, sucker Punch’s follow-up to Ghost of Tsushima is everything you could want in a sequel. The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym.
